lessons.title: Definition and Scope of Government
lessons.objective: Define government, distinguish it from the state, and explain why its scope covers the functions only public authority can perform.

content.heading: Government in one sentence
paragraphs: Government is the set of institutions that make, enforce and interpret binding rules for a society. Its scope is the work that needs public authority: keeping order, providing public goods and acting for the state.

content.heading: A bridge no business will rebuild
paragraphs: A bridge on a rural road collapses after heavy rain. Drivers cannot cross, farmers cannot move produce, and no private firm will rebuild it because it cannot charge every user. The council, state or federal agency with the road must act.

Government is the institution that makes, enforces and interprets the rules of a society. Its characteristics include a defined jurisdiction, a hierarchy of offices, taxing power and a claim to a monopoly on legitimate force.

It acts through three arms: the legislature makes law, the executive carries it out, and the judiciary settles disputes and interprets the law. Government is not the state; the state is the permanent political community of territory, population, government and sovereignty, while government is the replaceable machinery that rules it.
bullets: Government makes, enforces and interprets binding rules.
It has a defined jurisdiction and a hierarchy of offices.
It claims a monopoly on the legitimate use of force.
Its three arms are the legislature, executive and judiciary.
content.takeaway: Government is the ruling machinery of a permanent state.

check.question: Which of these is a characteristic of government rather than a function?
options: It has a defined jurisdiction and a hierarchy of offices.
It defends the country against attack.
check.why: A defined jurisdiction and hierarchy describe what government is; the others are services it provides.

content.heading: Why the bridge is not a business
paragraphs: Markets supply most of what people want: traders sell food, builders put up houses and banks lend money. Some goods are different. A defence force, a street light or a drainage system cannot easily be sold to one buyer, and everyone benefits whether they pay or not.

Government keeps law and order and protects life and property. It defends the territory, conducts relations with other states and provides public goods such as roads, schools, health care, water and security.
It also protects rights, regulates the economy and settles disputes. Taxes pay for these functions, which is why government must raise revenue.
bullets: Public goods are shared and hard to charge for, so markets under-supply them.
Government also protects rights and limits harm that markets ignore.
Taxes turn private income into shared public functions.
content.takeaway: Government does what markets cannot do fairly or profitably.

check.question: A private firm will not build a rural bridge because it cannot charge every user. Which function does this illustrate?
check.why: The bridge is shared and hard to charge for, so government supplies it as a public good.

content.heading: The coup that changed the government
paragraphs: In January 1966, soldiers took over Nigeria's government. The flag, territory, population and international borders stayed; the rulers changed. A coup replaces a government, not the state.

The state is the permanent political community: territory, population, government and sovereignty. Government is the temporary set of institutions that exercises the state's authority, which is why one state can have many governments.

The distinction also fixes the scope. Government acts for the state but does not own it, and its powers are limited by the constitution. In Nigeria, that scope is divided among federal, state and local tiers.
bullets: The state is permanent; a government is replaceable.
Government exercises the state's authority within constitutional limits.
Its scope is divided among federal, state and local tiers.
Public office is not private ownership.
content.takeaway: The state outlives the government that acts for it.

check.question: A coup removes a president and his ministers. What has changed?
check.why: A coup replaces rulers; the state's territory, population and sovereignty remain.

visual.caption: The state is the permanent community; the government is the machinery that rules it.

rows.left: Does it survive a change of rulers?
rows.right: Does it make and enforce rules?

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a question asks about government, reject options that describe the state: permanent, sovereign, or defined by territory and population. Government is the replaceable machinery that makes and enforces rules for a society.

content.problem: Which statement best distinguishes government from the state? A. Government is permanent while the state changes B. The state is the ruling machinery while government is the community C. Government is the machinery that rules the state, which is permanent D. Government and the state are the same thing

steps.reason: The state is the permanent political community; government is the machinery that rules it.
steps.result: Look for an option that keeps that direction.
steps.predictPrompt: Which term survives a change of rulers?

steps.reason: The state survives changes of rulers, so any option calling government permanent is wrong.
steps.result: Options A and D fail.

steps.reason: Government acts for the state; the state is not the machinery of government.
steps.result: Option C is correct.

content.question: A newly elected government promises to build roads, fund schools and defend the border. Explain why these are government functions rather than ordinary business activities. Then state one function that a private firm could perform.
hints: Ask whether the service can be sold to one buyer and withheld from others.
Defence and roads benefit people who do not pay, so markets under-supply them.
A private firm can build houses, sell food or run a bus service, but it needs the legal order that government maintains.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the state outlives its government
paragraphs: Permanence is a legal idea, not a physical one. A state continues when its government falls because its territory, population, constitution and international obligations continue. Other states recognise the state, not the regime.

This continuity matters in practice. Treaties signed by one government bind its successors, public debt survives a change of government, and civil servants, courts and police remain when ministers leave. A new government inherits both assets and obligations.

Sovereignty belongs to the state, not to the officeholder. The government exercises it for the time being: it makes treaties, declares war and passes laws, but it does not own the state's territory or people. That is why a coup can be illegal and still leave the state intact.

Exam questions often test this by asking what changes after a coup. The rulers change; the state's territory, population and sovereignty do not. The same logic explains why a country can lose its government without losing its statehood.
bullets: Treaties, debts and borders survive a change of government.
Sovereignty belongs to the state; the government exercises it temporarily.
A coup changes rulers, not statehood.

content.heading: Go deeper: Public goods and the limits of markets
paragraphs: A public good has two features: one person's use does not reduce another's, and non-payers cannot easily be excluded. Defence, street lighting and flood control are close examples. Because a firm cannot charge every beneficiary, it cannot recover the cost, so the good is under-supplied without public funding.

Some goods are not pure public goods but create externalities. A factory that pollutes imposes a cost on neighbours who did not agree to it. Government can tax the pollution, regulate the factory or require compensation, so that the private decision faces its social cost.

Other functions rest on coordination and trust. Courts settle disputes because private enforcement invites revenge, and standards for weights, measures and money reduce the cost of every transaction. Regulation of banks protects depositors who cannot inspect a balance sheet.

The scope is not unlimited. Government may fail too: monopolies can be inefficient, officials can be corrupt, and subsidies can outlive their purpose. The exam point is not that government should do everything, but that some functions cannot be left to a market alone.
bullets: Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable, so markets under-supply them.
Externalities and information gaps justify regulation.
Government failure limits what the state should attempt.

content.heading: Go deeper: Who does what in a federation
paragraphs: Nigeria divides government functions between federal, state and local tiers. The constitution lists exclusive functions for the federal government, such as defence, currency and foreign affairs. It lists concurrent functions for federal and state governments, such as education and health.

Residual functions go to the states, and local governments handle local services such as markets and refuse. The division is a scope rule. When a road is federal, a state government that rebuilds it may be acting outside its lane; when a market is local, the federal government should not run it directly.

In practice the tiers share costs and responsibilities, which blurs the line. States with more people and land may need more roads, while states with more taxable activity can raise more revenue. Federal transfers try to close the gap, but they also create dependence.
For exams, separate the two questions. First ask what the function is; then ask which tier has the power to perform it. A question about local government is usually testing the second.
bullets: Exclusive, concurrent and residual functions divide the tiers' scope.
The tier with the power may still share the cost.
Ask what the function is before asking who performs it.

lessons.title: Basic Concepts of Government
lessons.objective: Distinguish power, authority, legitimacy and sovereignty, and tell a state from a nation.

content.heading: Power, authority and the state
paragraphs: Power is the ability to make others act; authority is power accepted as rightful; legitimacy is the belief that justifies it. Sovereignty is supreme power, and a state is the political organisation that holds it over a territory and people.

content.heading: Power and influence
paragraphs: Power is the ability to affect others' behaviour, even against their will. It may rest on force, wealth, office, information or persuasion. Influence is the quieter form: shaping what others think or do without commanding them.
bullets: Power is the capacity to compel; influence is the capacity to shape without compulsion.
Sources of power include force, wealth, office, knowledge, charisma and numbers.
Power need not be legitimate: a coup leader may hold power while lacking authority.

content.heading: Authority and legitimacy
paragraphs: Authority is power accepted as rightful. A teacher may be able to punish, but authority exists when students accept that the punishment is deserved. Authority therefore rests on belief, not simply on force.

Legitimacy is that belief. A government is legitimate when people accept that it has the right to rule, even when they disagree with it. Legitimacy turns obedience from fear into duty, so legitimate governments need less coercion.
By source, authority is traditional (custom), charismatic (personal appeal) or legal-rational (law and office); modern states rely mainly on the last, so authority attaches to the office.
bullets: Power is ability; authority is accepted right; legitimacy is the belief that the right is real.
Traditional, charismatic and legal-rational authority differ by source.
A government can hold power without legitimacy — the usual position after an unpopular coup.

visual.caption: Legitimacy is the belief that turns power into authority.

rows.left: The ability to make others act

rows.right: Belief that the right to command is real
Do people obey because they accept the right?

rows.left: A coup leader with the army
rows.right: A government whose orders are accepted

content.heading: Sovereignty
paragraphs: Sovereignty is supreme and final authority within a territory. Internal sovereignty means the state is the highest authority over its people and institutions; external sovereignty means it is independent of other states.

Legal sovereignty belongs to the body that makes final law — the constitution or parliament. Popular sovereignty belongs to the people, exercised through elections and referendums; the constitution organises how that power is used.
bullets: Internal sovereignty is supremacy at home; external sovereignty is independence abroad.
Legal sovereignty sits with the constitution or parliament; popular sovereignty sits with the people.
Sovereignty is limited in practice by treaties, international law and economic dependence.

content.heading: State, nation and nation-state
paragraphs: A state has four elements: territory, population, government and sovereignty. A nation is a group of people sharing an identity — language, history, culture or belonging. A nation-state exists when borders roughly match a nation’s identity.
The two often diverge. Nigeria is a state containing many nations; the Kurds are a nation without a state. Society is the wider web of relationships; the state is its political organisation.
bullets: State = territory + population + government + sovereignty.
Nation = shared identity; state = political organisation; nation-state = both coincide.
A state can contain many nations; a nation can exist without a state.

content.heading: Political processes
paragraphs: Political socialisation is how people learn political attitudes and behaviour. Family, school, media, religion, peers and parties are its agents. It is how a child born without political opinions becomes a citizen who holds them.

Political participation is activity through which people take part: voting, campaigning, protesting, contacting officials and standing for office. Political culture is the pattern of beliefs and values a society holds about politics — for example, whether authority is trusted or suspected.
bullets: Socialisation forms attitudes; participation expresses them; culture is the shared pattern they form.
Agents of socialisation include family, school, media, religion, peers and parties.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a question asks where authority is vested, name the source of legitimacy — the state or the people — not an agent such as the judiciary or the police.

content.problem: Political authority is vested in the ______.

steps.reason: Authority is legitimate power — the right to command.
steps.result: Find the body that owns political power, not one of its agents.
steps.predictPrompt: Is the judiciary the source of authority or an arm that exercises it?

steps.reason: The state holds sovereign authority over the political community.
steps.result: Authority is vested in the state.

steps.reason: The judiciary, executive and armed forces exercise authority but do not own it.
steps.result: The state is the answer.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why legitimacy is harder to keep than to win
paragraphs: Legality and legitimacy are not the same. A law can be passed correctly and still be rejected as illegitimate if the process or the rulers are seen as unfair. Courts decide legality; people decide legitimacy. A government that confuses the two keeps winning cases while losing obedience.

Legitimacy has several sources. Input legitimacy comes from how power is won and exercised: free elections, the rule of law, consent. Output legitimacy comes from what government delivers: security, schools, roads, economic stability. A government can survive a deficit in one if the other is strong, but rarely both.

Coups expose the difference. A coup leader may control the army, the radio and the treasury — full power — yet lack authority, because no accepted rule makes his command rightful. To convert power into authority he must win recognition: from citizens, from other states, and often from an election.

Legitimacy is also cheaper than coercion. A legitimate government collects taxes, enforces court orders and recruits soldiers with less force, because people comply voluntarily. Once legitimacy erodes, every policy costs more to enforce.
bullets: Legality is decided by courts; legitimacy is decided by belief and consent.
Input legitimacy comes from how power is won; output legitimacy from what it delivers.
A coup can seize power without acquiring authority.
Legitimacy lowers the cost of governing because compliance becomes voluntary.

content.heading: Go deeper: Sovereignty in a world of interdependence
paragraphs: Sovereignty sounds absolute, but no modern state exercises it without limits. A state joins the United Nations and accepts its charter; it signs treaties that bind future governments; it borrows money on conditions set by lenders. Each commitment is a voluntary limit on external sovereignty.

Pooled sovereignty is the formal name for this. Members of ECOWAS, the African Union and the United Nations delegate some decisions to collective bodies in exchange for influence and protection. Nigeria can shape ECOWAS decisions, but it must also accept decisions it dislikes.

Internal sovereignty is constrained too. Federalism divides authority between national and state governments; constitutions entrench rights that no majority may remove; independent courts can strike down laws. These are not failures of sovereignty but its organisation.

Economic dependence adds a harder limit. Debt service, import dependence and foreign investment give outsiders leverage over budgets and policy. A state may be legally sovereign and still have little room to choose.
bullets: Treaties and international organisations voluntarily limit external sovereignty.
Federalism, entrenched rights and judicial review divide internal sovereignty by design.
Legal sovereignty does not guarantee policy freedom when the economy is dependent.

content.heading: Go deeper: Reading political culture and participation
paragraphs: Political culture is not opinion polling. It is the durable pattern of beliefs about authority, participation and the state. Almond and Verba distinguished parochial culture, where people barely identify with the state; subject culture, where they obey but do not participate; and participant culture, where they expect to influence decisions.

Most states mix the three. A village may be parochial about national politics while a capital city is participant. The mix explains why the same constitution produces different behaviour in different places.

Participation is shaped by resources and institutions. Educated, urban and organised citizens vote, lobby and protest more; proportional systems and strong parties raise turnout; repression lowers it. Low turnout is therefore not always apathy — it can be a rational response to institutions that do not respond.
For exams, keep the map clean: socialisation explains how attitudes form, culture describes the pattern, participation describes the action.
bullets: Parochial, subject and participant cultures differ in whether people identify, obey or engage.
Most states contain a mixture of cultures rather than one pure type.
Participation tracks resources and institutions, not just individual interest.
Socialisation → culture → participation is the causal chain to remember.

content.question: A traditional ruler is obeyed because people believe his office is rightful. Is that power, authority or legitimacy? Explain in one sentence.
hints: Power is the ability to influence; authority is accepted power.
The people accept the office as rightful — that belief is legitimacy.
The best answer names authority and explains that legitimacy is the belief supporting it.

lessons.title: Forms and Systems of Government
lessons.objective: Tell forms of government apart and distinguish presidential from parliamentary systems.

content.heading: Forms of government
paragraphs: A form of government answers the question: who rules? A system of government answers: how do the organs relate?
bullets: Democracy: rule by the people, usually through elected representatives.
Monarchy: rule by a king or queen; absolute or constitutional.
Aristocracy: rule by a small group considered the best.
Oligarchy: rule by a few powerful people; plutocracy is rule by the wealthy.
Autocracy: one person holds unlimited power; republicanism has an elected head, not a hereditary one.

content.heading: Presidential and parliamentary systems
paragraphs: In a presidential system the executive and legislature are separate and separately elected. In a parliamentary system the executive comes from the legislature and depends on its confidence.
bullets: Presidential: fixed term, separation of powers, president is both head of state and government.
Parliamentary: prime minister leads, cabinet ministers are usually MPs, and a vote of no confidence can bring the government down.
Monarchical systems may be absolute (the monarch rules) or constitutional (the monarch reigns but does not rule).
The key exam difference is separation of powers: presidential systems separate the executive from the legislature; parliamentary systems fuse them.

visual.caption: Where the executive comes from decides how it can be removed.

rows.right: Lasts while it holds the legislature's confidence
The UK's prime minister and Parliament

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Form = who rules. System = how the arms relate. Read the question carefully before choosing.

content.problem: The major difference between the presidential and parliamentary systems is ______.

steps.reason: In a presidential system the president is elected separately from the legislature.
steps.result: The executive does not sit in the legislature or depend on its confidence.
steps.predictPrompt: What happens to a prime minister who loses a vote of no confidence?

steps.reason: A parliamentary executive is drawn from and answerable to parliament.
steps.result: The executive and legislature are fused, not separated.

steps.reason: The difference is the separation of powers.
steps.result: Choose the option that says separation of powers.

content.question: Nigeria uses a presidential system. Name one advantage and one disadvantage of separating the executive from the legislature.
hints: Separation can protect liberty and prevent one arm from dominating.
It can also produce gridlock when the president and legislature belong to different parties.
A strong answer gives one benefit (checks and balances) and one cost (deadlock).

lessons.title: Arms of Government
lessons.objective: Match each arm to its types, functions and powers, and explain how the three arms check one another.

content.heading: Three arms, one government
paragraphs: The legislature makes law, the executive implements it, and the judiciary interprets it. Separation of powers also lets each arm check the others, so no arm governs alone.

content.heading: A bill on rural roads
paragraphs: A senator proposes a bill to fund rural roads. It is introduced, debated, examined in committee and passed by both chambers. Assent turns it into an Act; a veto can be overridden.

The legislature is the law-making arm. It may be unicameral, with one chamber, or bicameral, with two. Nigeria's National Assembly has a Senate and a House of Representatives, and each state has a House of Assembly.

It makes, amends and repeals laws, approves the budget, oversees public spending and represents constituencies; the Senate confirms appointments. A bill passes first reading, second reading, committee stage and third reading before assent.
In Britain Parliament is supreme; in Nigeria the Constitution is supreme, so the National Assembly cannot make any law it likes.
bullets: The legislature makes, amends and repeals laws.
Nigeria has a bicameral National Assembly: Senate and House of Representatives.
Debate begins at second reading; assent makes a bill an Act.
content.takeaway: The legislature makes law, but assent and the Constitution limit it.

check.question: At which stage does debate on a bill begin?
check.why: First reading is a formal introduction; debate begins at second reading.

content.heading: The ministry must build the road
paragraphs: The Act is law, but the road is still unbuilt. A ministry plans it, the civil service drafts the contract, and the police keep order. The executive turns law into action.

The executive implements laws and runs the country day to day. It may be presidential, with a president who is both head of state and government, or parliamentary, with a prime minister leading a cabinet from the legislature.
It conducts foreign relations, defends the territory, prepares the budget and appoints officials. It checks the legislature through assent and veto, and it makes delegated legislation under statute.

The civil service is the permanent body of officials in ministries; it is part of the wider public service, which also includes the police, armed forces and parastatals. Implementing government programmes is its primary duty.
bullets: The executive implements laws and runs government day to day.
Political executive = elected ministers; administrative executive = civil service.
Civil service = permanent ministry officials; public service = the wider body.
content.takeaway: The executive turns law into administration.

check.question: The executive checks the legislature mainly through ______.
check.why: The president can sign or withhold assent; treaties and orders are other executive powers.

content.heading: The court reads the Act
paragraphs: A contractor is denied payment and sues the ministry. The court reads the Act, examines the minister's decision and orders payment. It interpreted the law and checked the executive.

The judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes. Its components are the courts: the Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, Federal High Court, State High Courts, Sharia and Customary Courts of Appeal, and tribunals.

It interprets the Constitution, protects rights, punishes offenders and reviews government action. Judicial review lets it declare a law or executive act unconstitutional, which checks both other arms.

Judicial independence means judges decide without legislative or executive pressure. Security of tenure, salaries charged to the Consolidated Revenue Fund and appointment through the Federal Judicial Service Commission and National Judicial Council protect it.
bullets: The judiciary interprets laws, protects rights and reviews government action.
Judicial review can void an unconstitutional law or executive act.
Independence means no legislative or executive pressure on decisions.
FJSC nominates federal judges; NJC recommends them to the President.
content.takeaway: The judiciary interprets the law and checks both other arms.

check.question: The independence of the judiciary means that ______.
options: judges must ignore legislative and executive affairs
court decisions cannot be reviewed by any higher court
legislative and executive influence on judicial decisions must be prevented
judges must be protected from public criticism
check.why: Independence protects the decision, not the judge from criticism or appeal.

visual.caption: A bill crosses all three arms: the legislature passes it, the executive assents and implements, the courts interpret.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In Nigeria the Constitution is supreme, not the legislature. A bill needs both chambers and presidential assent, or an override of a veto; a court can later strike down the Act if it conflicts with the Constitution.

content.problem: A bill passes both chambers but the president refuses assent. What happens next? A. It becomes law after thirty days B. It fails unless the National Assembly overrides the veto C. The Supreme Court signs it D. State governors assent

steps.reason: The bill has passed both chambers but lacks assent.
steps.result: It is not yet an Act.
steps.predictPrompt: Who signs a federal bill into law?

steps.reason: A two-thirds majority of each chamber can override a presidential veto.
steps.result: The bill can still become law.

steps.reason: Courts do not sign bills and governors do not assent to federal bills.
steps.result: Option B is correct.

content.question: Name the arm that makes laws and the arm that implements them. Then explain one check each arm has on the other.
hints: The legislature makes law; the executive implements it.
The executive can assent to or veto a bill; the legislature can override a veto or refuse to confirm appointments.
The judiciary can review both laws and executive action.

content.heading: Go deeper: How a bill becomes law in Nigeria
paragraphs: A bill is a proposed law. In Nigeria, it may be introduced in either chamber of the National Assembly, except a money bill, which starts in the House of Representatives.

The first reading is a formal introduction; no debate takes place. Debate begins at the second reading, where members discuss the general principles. The committee stage then examines the clauses in detail, and the report stage brings the amended bill back to the chamber.
The third reading is the final passage vote. The other chamber must concur, and any disagreement is resolved by a conference committee. The bill then goes to the president for assent.

If the president withholds assent, he returns it with reasons. The National Assembly can override the veto by a two-thirds majority of each chamber, and the bill becomes law. A state bill follows the same path through the State House of Assembly and the governor.
Courts do not make the bill law, but they may later interpret it or declare it unconstitutional. That is why the process is a chain across the three arms, not a single legislative act.
bullets: First reading introduces; second reading debates; committee stage examines clauses.
Both chambers must agree before assent.
A two-thirds majority in each chamber can override a presidential veto.

content.heading: Go deeper: Presidential and parliamentary executives
paragraphs: In a presidential system, the president is both head of state and head of government, and the executive is separately elected from the legislature. In a parliamentary system, the prime minister is head of government while a monarch or ceremonial president is head of state.

The parliamentary executive is drawn from the legislature and survives only while it holds the confidence of the majority. A vote of no confidence can bring it down, and the prime minister may dissolve parliament and call an election. The presidential executive has a fixed term and cannot be removed by a simple vote of no confidence.

Nigeria operates a presidential system: the president is elected separately, appoints ministers with Senate confirmation, and serves a fixed four-year term. Britain operates a parliamentary system: the prime minister normally leads the party with a majority in the House of Commons.

The difference shapes the checks. A presidential president can veto legislation but may face an override; a prime minister usually controls the legislative programme because the executive sits in the legislature. Neither system removes the need for judicial review.
bullets: Presidential: separate election, fixed term, president is head of state and government.
Parliamentary: executive from the legislature; a confidence vote can remove it.
Nigeria is presidential; Britain is parliamentary.

content.heading: Go deeper: Judicial independence and the appointment of judges
paragraphs: Judicial independence has two sides: the courts must be free from interference, and judges must be accountable to the law. Nigeria protects the first through security of tenure, salaries charged to the Consolidated Revenue Fund, and a disciplined removal process.

Federal judicial appointments begin with the Federal Judicial Service Commission, which advises the National Judicial Council on nominees. The NJC recommends candidates to the President, and the Senate confirms the senior federal appointments, including the Chief Justice of Nigeria and the justices of the Supreme Court.

State appointments follow a similar path through the State Judicial Service Commission and the governor, with the NJC involved and the State House of Assembly confirming the Chief Judge. The process is designed to keep patronage out of the bench, though critics say it remains political.

Independence does not mean judges ignore the law or answer to no one. They can be removed for misconduct, and their decisions can be appealed. What it forbids is a president or legislature punishing a judge for an unpopular ruling.

The judiciary also checks the other arms through judicial review. It can declare a statute unconstitutional, quash an executive action, or order a public body to act lawfully. That power is strongest when judges are seen to be independent, because a ruling that looks politically dictated loses authority.
bullets: Tenure, protected salaries and a removal process shield judges from pressure.
The FJSC advises; the NJC recommends; the Senate confirms senior appointments.
Independence means freedom from interference, not freedom from the law.

lessons.title: Constitution and the Rule of Law
lessons.objective: Explain what a constitution does, compare written and unwritten constitutions, and apply the rule of law.

content.heading: What a constitution is
paragraphs: A constitution contains the fundamental laws that establish government, distribute power and limit it. It is the supreme law: every other law must conform to it.
bullets: Sources: statutes, conventions, judicial decisions, custom and authoritative texts.
Functions: establish institutions, distribute power, protect rights and provide stability.
Written constitutions are usually codified in one document; unwritten constitutions rest on statutes, conventions and common law.
Rigid constitutions are hard to amend; flexible ones can be changed by ordinary law.

content.heading: The rule of law
paragraphs: The rule of law means that the law is supreme over every person and institution, including the government. It operates in states where laws, not officials, are supreme.
bullets: Supremacy of the law: no punishment without a breach of law.
Equality before the law: everyone is subject to the same courts.
Individual rights are protected by ordinary courts.
Separation of powers and checks and balances help prevent arbitrary rule.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: The rule of law is not limited to democracies or developing countries. It applies wherever laws are supreme and officials are answerable to them.

content.problem: An example of a country with an unwritten constitution is ______.

steps.reason: An unwritten constitution is not collected in one codified document.
steps.result: It is found in statutes, conventions and court decisions.
steps.predictPrompt: Which country is famous for this arrangement?

steps.reason: The United Kingdom has no single written constitutional document.
steps.result: The United Kingdom is the standard example.

steps.reason: Nigeria, the USA and Sierra Leone have written constitutions.
steps.result: Choose the United Kingdom.

content.question: A governor ignores a court order because he controls the police. Which rule-of-law principle has he broken, and why?
hints: The rule of law requires everyone, including officials, to obey the law.
Ignoring a court order attacks the supremacy of the law and equality before it.
A strong answer names supremacy of the law and explains that no official is above it.

lessons.title: Pre-colonial and Colonial Administration
lessons.objective: Compare the Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa/Fulani systems and trace the colonial constitutions to independence.

content.heading: Pre-colonial systems
paragraphs: The three major pre-colonial systems were organised differently. The Yoruba were monarchical, the Igbo were largely acephalous and consensual, and the Hausa/Fulani were theocratic and centralised.
bullets: Yoruba: the Oba ruled with the Oyomesi (chiefs) and the Ogboni cult; the Alaafin of Oyo was checked by the Oyomesi.
Igbo: the village assembly (Oha-na-eze), the Okpara (oldest man), age grades and title societies made decisions by consensus.
Hausa/Fulani: the Emir ruled a theocratic emirate; the Galadima administered the capital, the Madaki commanded the army and the Alkali judged cases.

content.heading: Colonial rule and the constitutions
paragraphs: Colonial administration moved from company rule to direct Crown control, then through a series of constitutions that widened Nigerian participation.
bullets: Lagos was annexed as a Crown Colony in 1861.
The Royal Niger Company's charter was revoked in 1900, and Britain took direct control.
The Richards Constitution (1946) created regional councils and is said to have conceived federalism for Nigeria.
The Macpherson Constitution (1951) introduced ministerial government; the Lyttleton Constitution (1954) confirmed a federal structure with regional premiers.
Independence came in 1960; Nigeria became a republic in 1963.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Indirect rule preserved traditional authority but served colonial extraction. That dual effect explains both its administrative convenience and the rise of nationalism.

content.problem: Why is the Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 important?

steps.reason: Richards (1946) created regions; Macpherson (1951) added ministers; Lyttleton (1954) settled the federal shape.
steps.result: Lyttleton confirmed Nigeria as a federation.
steps.predictPrompt: What did it give each region?

steps.reason: The regions gained premiers and a larger share of power, while the centre handled federal matters.
steps.result: A federal structure with regional autonomy.

steps.reason: The constitution's key legacy is the federal structure.
steps.result: Choose the option that says it confirmed Nigeria as a federal structure.

content.question: Give one difference between the Yoruba and Igbo pre-colonial systems, and one reason the difference mattered to colonial administrators.
hints: The Yoruba had a central Oba; the Igbo governed through village assemblies and consensus.
Indirect rule needed a single ruler to deal with — that was easier where a monarchy existed.
A strong answer contrasts centralised monarchy with acephalous consensus and links it to indirect rule.

lessons.title: Political Parties, Pressure Groups and Elections
lessons.objective: Explain what parties do, compare party systems, distinguish parties from pressure groups, and describe free elections.

content.heading: Parties and party systems
paragraphs: A political party is an organised group that seeks to win elections and control government. Its manifesto sets out what it would do in office.
bullets: Functions: aggregate interests, recruit and train leaders, formulate policy, mobilise voters, organise government and provide opposition scrutiny.
A national party draws members from across ethnic and regional lines, not just branches in many places.
One-party system: only one party is legal or effective. Two-party system: two parties alternate in power. Multi-party system: several parties compete, often in coalitions.
A dominant-party system is competitive in law but one party wins repeatedly in practice.

content.heading: Pressure groups and elections
paragraphs: Pressure groups try to influence policy without seeking to govern. Elections are the main channel through which citizens choose who governs.
bullets: Pressure-group methods: lobbying, petitions, publicity, dialogue, strikes and, as a last resort, an ultimatum with a deadline.
Franchise is the right to vote; a constituency is the area that elects a representative.
A referendum is a direct vote on a specific issue; a plebiscite is similar but often advisory.
Free and fair elections need an independent electoral commission, a credible register, a secret ballot and an impartial judiciary to settle disputes.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Parties contest elections in order to govern. Pressure groups influence whoever governs but do not put up a government of their own.

content.problem: Market traders demand that a new levy be withdrawn and threaten a strike if it is not done within seven days. Are they acting as a party or a pressure group, and which tactic are they using?

steps.reason: A party contests elections to govern; a pressure group only wants to change a decision.
steps.result: The traders are acting as a pressure group.
steps.predictPrompt: Which of their actions is the final tactic?

steps.reason: A demand with a deadline and a threatened strike is the strongest pressure-group step.
steps.result: They have issued an ultimatum.

steps.reason: If the deadline passes, the threatened strike becomes the action; dialogue and lobbying come earlier.
steps.result: The sequence runs lobbying → dialogue → ultimatum → strike.

content.question: Why does a party need membership across ethnic lines to be truly national, and why is having branches everywhere not enough?
hints: Branches can exist in every state while membership and leadership remain tied to one ethnic or regional group.
A national party must be able to aggregate interests from many groups, not just represent one.
A strong answer links ethnic breadth to winning a national majority and to legitimacy.

lessons.title: Foreign Policy and International Organisations
lessons.objective: Explain Nigeria’s foreign-policy goals and the roles and decision rules of ECOWAS, the African Union and the United Nations.

content.heading: Nigeria’s foreign policy
paragraphs: Foreign policy is a state’s strategy for dealing with other states and international organisations. Nigeria’s has been Afrocentric since independence.
bullets: Goals: defend sovereignty and territory, promote African decolonisation and unity, support peace and security, and pursue economic development.
Principles: Afrocentrism, non-alignment, sovereign equality, non-interference and peaceful settlement of disputes.
Instruments: diplomacy, foreign aid, military support, trade and membership of multilateral bodies.
The Murtala/Obasanjo era reviewed policy toward a more assertive, Africa-centred stance; the Bakassi dispute with Cameroon was decided by the International Court of Justice in 2002.

content.heading: International organisations
paragraphs: Nigeria belongs to global and regional bodies. Each has different members, powers and decision rules.
bullets: UN: the General Assembly is the most representative organ, with one vote per member. The Security Council has five permanent members with a veto and primary responsibility for peace and security. The ICJ settles legal disputes between states; the Secretariat administers the UN.
African Union: replaced the OAU in 2002. The Executive Council generally decides by consensus, falling back on a two-thirds majority.
ECOWAS: founded in 1975 by the Treaty of Lagos to promote trade, free movement and regional peacekeeping (ECOMOG). Its chairmanship rotates.
Commonwealth and OPEC: the Commonwealth links former British colonies; OPEC coordinates oil-exporting states to stabilise prices.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: The General Assembly is the most representative UN organ because every member has one vote. The Security Council is the most powerful, not the most representative.

content.problem: Nigeria has a legal boundary dispute with a neighbour and wants a binding judgment. Which UN organ should hear it, and why not the Security Council?

steps.reason: A boundary dispute is a legal question between states, not a threat to peace requiring enforcement.
steps.result: It belongs to judicial settlement.
steps.predictPrompt: Which organ decides legal disputes between states?

steps.reason: The International Court of Justice hears contentious cases between states and gives binding judgments.
steps.result: Nigeria should take the case to the ICJ.

steps.operation: Explain the limit of the Security Council
steps.reason: The Security Council deals with peace and security and can impose sanctions, but it does not adjudicate boundary law.
steps.result: The ICJ supplies the legal ruling; the Security Council may later help enforce peace if needed.

content.question: Name two benefits of ECOWAS membership to Nigeria and one cost, then say whether the benefits outweigh the cost.
hints: Benefits: a larger market for Nigerian goods, free movement of people, and joint peacekeeping that stabilises the region.
Costs: contributions to the community budget, pressure from migration, and limits on unilateral policy.
A strong answer weighs the market and security gains against funding and sovereignty costs.

lessons.title: Citizenship: Acquisition, Rights and Loss
lessons.objective: Differentiate the routes to citizenship, separate rights from duties, state what the state owes, and explain dual citizenship, renunciation and deprivation.

content.heading: Citizenship in one sentence
paragraphs: Citizenship is the legal bond between a person and a state, and it carries rights, duties and protection that residence alone never creates.

content.heading: A girl born in Lagos, a woman married in Kano
paragraphs: A girl is born in Lagos to parents from Enugu, and a woman marries a Nigerian in Kano; both are citizens. A trader from Chad has lived in Nigeria for twenty years, yet he remains an alien, because citizenship follows law rather than length of stay.

Section 25 grants citizenship by birth: born in Nigeria before independence to a parent or grandparent from an indigenous community, or born in Nigeria after independence to a citizen parent or grandparent. The fourth route, descent, covers a person born outside Nigeria to a citizen parent.
Registration covers a woman married to a citizen; naturalisation covers an adult foreigner of good character who has lived in Nigeria for fifteen years and takes the oath of allegiance.
bullets: Birth: born in Nigeria to a citizen parent or grandparent.
Descent: born abroad to a citizen parent.
Registration for marriage; naturalisation after fifteen years.
content.takeaway: Citizenship is acquired by law, not by residence or property.

check.question: A man born in Ghana to Nigerian parents has never lived in Nigeria. His status is ______.
options: a citizen only after fifteen years
check.why: A person born outside Nigeria to a citizen parent is a citizen by descent; residence is irrelevant.

content.heading: The right to speak, the duty to pay
paragraphs: A trader criticises a governor on radio, then pays his market levy. The criticism is protected by Chapter IV of the Constitution; the levy is a duty under section 24.

Chapter IV rights include life, dignity, personal liberty, fair hearing, private and family life, thought and conscience, expression, peaceful assembly, movement, property and freedom from discrimination. They bind government and can be enforced in court.

Section 24 duties are to respect the Constitution and national symbols, respect other people's rights, assist lawful agencies, pay taxes and defend Nigeria when required. The state must also protect rights and pursue welfare and security under Chapter II, though those goals are not directly enforceable.
bullets: Rights are claims the citizen can enforce against the state.
Duties are obligations owed to the state and to other citizens.
Freedom of conscience is a right, not a civil obligation.
content.takeaway: Rights protect the person; duties protect the state and other citizens.

check.question: Which of these is a duty of a Nigerian citizen?
check.why: Paying tax is a section 24 duty; conscience, fair hearing and movement are Chapter IV rights.

content.heading: A Canadian passport, a renunciation
paragraphs: A naturalised citizen acquires Canadian citizenship and loses Nigerian citizenship; a citizen by birth who does the same keeps it. Section 28 protects dual citizenship for citizens by birth; a new nationality ends the other routes.

Renunciation is voluntary: a citizen of full age declares that he or she is giving up the status, and the President registers the declaration, though he may refuse during a war. Deprivation is imposed by the state, mainly for disloyalty, trading with the enemy, or a long prison sentence soon after naturalisation.

The state's side is protection: security at home, consular help abroad, and welfare, education and health under Chapter II. A person who loses citizenship loses its rights, though many Chapter IV rights protect everyone in Nigeria.
bullets: Birth citizenship allows a second passport.
A new nationality ends citizenship by registration or naturalisation.
Renunciation is voluntary; deprivation is imposed for disloyalty or crime.
content.takeaway: Birth citizenship survives a second passport; registration and naturalisation do not.

check.question: A Nigerian who became a citizen by registration takes the citizenship of another country. What happens?
options: Citizenship is suspended for five years
check.why: Section 28: voluntarily taking a new nationality ends citizenship by registration or naturalisation, not birth.

visual.caption: Both end citizenship, but renunciation is the citizen's choice and deprivation is the state's decision.

rows.left: The citizen no longer wants the status
rows.right: Disloyalty, enemy trade or a long prison term

rows.left: Did the citizen choose to give it up?

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Property, residence and marriage do not by themselves make a citizen. Marriage opens registration; fifteen years' residence opens naturalisation; buying land opens nothing. Read the stem closely too: a civil obligation is a duty, so an option naming a right such as freedom of conscience is the exception.

content.problem: Classify each person: (a) a child born in Ibadan to parents from Ogun State; (b) a Lebanese trader born in Beirut who has lived in Kano for sixteen years and takes the oath; (c) a Nigerian-born engineer who also holds a British passport.

steps.reason: Birth in Nigeria to citizen parents is citizenship by birth under section 25.
steps.result: (a) Citizen by birth.
steps.predictPrompt: Does residence alone ever confer citizenship?

steps.reason: Sixteen years' residence, good character and the oath meet the naturalisation conditions.
steps.result: (b) Citizen by naturalisation.

steps.reason: A citizen by birth may hold another citizenship without losing Nigerian citizenship.
steps.result: (c) Still a Nigerian citizen.

content.question: A Nigerian citizen by birth takes a British passport. A naturalised Nigerian does the same. Explain what happens to each, and name one duty each still owes while a citizen.
hints: Section 28 permits dual citizenship for citizens by birth.
Registration and naturalisation end when another citizenship is voluntarily acquired.
Duties continue while citizenship lasts: obey the law, pay tax, respect national symbols, defend the country.

content.heading: Go deeper: The sections that decide citizenship
paragraphs: Chapter III of the 1999 Constitution is short but precise. Section 25 defines citizenship by birth; section 26 provides registration, chiefly for a woman married to a citizen and for a person of full age born outside Nigeria any of whose grandparents is a citizen; section 27 sets naturalisation. Sections 28 to 30 deal with dual citizenship, renunciation and deprivation.

Naturalisation is not a formality. The applicant must be of full age and capacity, of good character, intend to be domiciled in Nigeria, be acceptable to the local community, be capable of contributing to national development, take the oath and show fifteen years' continuous residence or fifteen years in the aggregate over the preceding twenty. The President grants the certificate.

The rules are not gender-neutral. A foreign woman married to a Nigerian may register, while a foreign husband must naturalise, and the 1999 text makes no provision for foundlings or adopted children to acquire citizenship. Statelessness monitors have criticised both gaps.

Renunciation is the citizen's own act under section 29: an adult declares the intention, and the President registers it, though registration may be refused during a war or where it is contrary to public policy.

Section 28 withdraws citizenship from a registered or naturalised citizen who acquires or keeps a nationality of which he is not a citizen by birth, and section 30 allows deprivation for disloyalty, trading with the enemy, or a prison sentence of three years or more within seven years of naturalisation. A citizen by birth keeps Nigerian citizenship after taking a second passport.
bullets: Sections 25 to 27 create the routes; 28 to 30 regulate dual status, renunciation and deprivation.
Naturalisation needs fifteen years' residence, good character, the oath and a contribution to development.
Foreign wives register; foreign husbands naturalise, an asymmetry critics want removed.

content.heading: Go deeper: Dual citizenship and public office
paragraphs: Dual citizenship is lawful in Nigeria, but not for everyone on the same terms. A citizen by birth may hold another nationality and travel on either passport; a citizen by registration or naturalisation cannot, because voluntary acquisition of another nationality ends the Nigerian status.

Public office sharpens the question. The President and state governors must be citizens by birth under sections 131 and 177, so a naturalised citizen cannot contest those offices even after decades of service. For other offices the Constitution requires citizenship, and election petitions have turned on whether a candidate lost it.

The practical trap is documentary. A candidate who naturalised abroad, or who renounced Nigerian citizenship and later reacquired it by registration, may satisfy the age and party tests yet fail the citizenship test. Read the constitutional text, not the passport in hand.

Dual citizenship also affects duties. A citizen abroad still owes allegiance, may be called to defend Nigeria, and remains liable to tax on Nigerian-source income. A second passport does not switch off section 24.
bullets: Birth citizens may hold a second passport; registered and naturalised citizens may not.
The President and governors must be citizens by birth.
A second passport does not cancel the duties of citizenship.

content.heading: Go deeper: What the state owes the citizen
paragraphs: The syllabus asks you to assess the obligations of the state, and the Constitution splits them in two. Chapter IV rights, from life and fair hearing to expression, movement and property, are enforceable: a citizen can sue a public officer who violates them. Chapter II duties, covering security, welfare, education and health, are directive principles that guide government but are not directly enforceable.

That distinction explains why an underfunded school rarely produces a successful lawsuit, while a detention without trial can be challenged at once. Section 14(2) still declares that the security and welfare of the people shall be the primary purpose of government, but section 6(6)(c) keeps Chapter II out of the courts.

Abroad, the state owes diplomatic and consular protection. A Nigerian arrested in another country can ask the embassy for help, though the embassy cannot override that country's courts. At home, the police and armed forces carry the duty to protect life and property, and their failure can ground a claim in damages.

The bargain is unequal but real: the citizen pays tax, obeys the law and may be conscripted; the state protects rights, provides security and pursues welfare. Exams reward the student who can say which side is enforceable.
bullets: Chapter IV rights are enforceable; Chapter II goals are not directly justiciable.
Section 14(2) makes security and welfare the primary purpose of government.
Consular protection abroad is part of the state's duty, but it cannot overturn foreign courts.

lessons.title: Political Ideologies: Capitalism, Socialism and the Rest
lessons.objective: Define ideology and distinguish capitalism, socialism, communism, liberalism, conservatism, feudalism and fascism.

content.heading: What an ideology is
paragraphs: An ideology is an organised set of beliefs about how political and economic life should be arranged: who should own wealth, how much the state should do, and how change should happen.
Most ideologies are placed on a spectrum by two questions: how much equality they want, and how much individual liberty they protect.
bullets: The left generally favours greater equality, public ownership and state action.
The right generally favours private property, markets and limited government.
The spectrum is a guide, not a law: parties mix positions in practice.

content.heading: The main ideologies
paragraphs: Exams test recognition: a short definition must map to the right label.
bullets: Capitalism: private ownership of the means of production, market prices and the profit motive.
Socialism: social or state ownership and planning, with equality as a central aim.
Communism: common ownership, a classless society, and in Marxist theory the eventual withering away of the state.
Liberalism: individual liberty, consent, limited government and gradual reform.
Conservatism: tradition, order, inherited institutions and caution about rapid change.
Feudalism: land held by a noble class and worked by peasants in return for service.
Fascism: extreme nationalism, a single leader and the subordination of the individual to the state, often resting on force.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Socialism and communism are not the same answer. Socialism allows private property and elections; communism envisages common ownership and a classless, stateless society.

content.problem: Name the ideology behind each statement: (a) “the state should own the banks and plan output”; (b) “we should keep our inherited institutions and change slowly”; (c) “land belongs to lords who grant it to peasants for service”.

steps.reason: State ownership plus planning is the socialist position.
steps.result: (a) Socialism.

steps.reason: Defending tradition and slow change is conservatism.
steps.result: (b) Conservatism.

steps.reason: Land-for-service between lords and peasants is feudalism.
steps.result: (c) Feudalism.

content.question: A country has extreme inequality. Which ideology would prescribe higher taxes and public ownership, and what is the strongest criticism of that prescription?
hints: Higher taxes and public ownership point to socialism or social democracy.
The criticism is usually about incentives, efficiency and state power.
A strong answer names the ideology and weighs the equality gain against the efficiency cost.

lessons.title: The Civil Service, Public Corporations and Local Government
lessons.objective: Explain the civil service, public corporations and local government, and distinguish political from administrative leadership.

content.heading: The civil service
paragraphs: The civil service is the permanent administrative arm of government. It turns policy into action and advises ministers.
bullets: Permanence: officials stay in post when governments change.
Neutrality: they serve whichever party is in power, without favour.
Anonymity: ministers take public credit and blame for policy.
Merit: recruitment and promotion are based on qualification, not party loyalty.
The minister is the political head of a ministry; the permanent secretary is its administrative head.
The Civil Service Commission handles appointment, promotion and discipline.

content.heading: Public corporations and local government
paragraphs: Not all public business is done through ministries. Corporations and councils have their own legal standing and functions.
bullets: A public corporation is created by statute as a separate legal person with its own board, accounts and powers.
It delivers services such as water, power or transport where a ministry would be too rigid.
Local government is the third tier, with elected councils and functions such as markets, local roads and sanitation.
Its largest revenue source since the 1976 reforms is statutory allocation from the Federation Account.
Traditional rulers exercise an advisory role in the modern system; they do not hold executive power.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: The minister is the political head; the permanent secretary is the administrative head. A question that says “administrative head” wants the permanent secretary.

content.problem: A state water board needs to sign a contract, and the ministry of water resources must brief the governor. Who has legal capacity to sign for the board, and who advises the governor?

steps.reason: A public corporation is a separate legal person, so it contracts in its own name.
steps.result: The board signs through its management, not the ministry.
steps.predictPrompt: Who gives the governor administrative advice?

steps.reason: The permanent secretary heads the ministry’s administration and advises on policy.
steps.result: The permanent secretary briefs the governor through the commissioner or minister.

steps.reason: Political direction and administrative execution are different functions.
steps.result: The board executes; the ministry advises and supervises.

content.question: Why does democracy need a politically neutral civil service, and what happens when it is not neutral?
hints: Governments change, but administration must continue without disruption.
A partisan service rewards loyalty over competence and politicises advice.
A strong answer links neutrality to continuity, impartial advice and public trust.

lessons.title: Nigerian Federalism and Military Rule
lessons.objective: Apply the federal principle, use the legislative lists, and explain how military rule shaped Nigeria’s federal structure.

content.heading: The federal principle
paragraphs: K. C. Wheare defined the federal principle as a division of powers between a general government and regional governments, each coordinate and independent within its own sphere.
Nigeria divides power using legislative lists, and the courts police the boundary.
bullets: Exclusive legislative list: only the federal government may legislate — defence, currency, foreign affairs.
Concurrent legislative list: both federal and state governments may legislate — education, health.
Residual list: matters left to the states.
Where federal and state laws conflict on a concurrent matter, the federal law prevails.
Other federal features: a written constitution, a bicameral legislature and a supreme court that arbitrates disputes.

content.heading: How Nigeria got here, and what military rule did
paragraphs: Nigerian federalism was built in stages and then reshaped by soldiers. Knowing the sequence answers most history questions.
bullets: 1914: amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates.
1946 Richards Constitution: conceived a federal structure with three regions.
1954 Lyttleton Constitution: established federalism with regional autonomy.
1960 independence, 1963 republic; 1967 twelve states, 1976 nineteen, 1987 twenty-one, 1991 thirty, 1996 thirty-six.
Military rule ran from 1966 to 1979 and from 1983 to 1999.

Military governments ruled by decree, suspended the constitution, ousted court jurisdiction and centralised power, which is why Nigeria is often called a federation with strong centralising tendencies.
The 1976 local government reforms gave councils a guaranteed share of the Federation Account.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: The 1946 Richards Constitution conceived federalism; the 1954 Lyttleton Constitution established it. Do not swap the two.

content.problem: The federal government sets a national minimum standard for secondary schools. A state passes a lower standard. Which law prevails, and on what basis?

steps.reason: Education is on the concurrent legislative list, so both levels may legislate.
steps.result: Both laws are within power.

steps.reason: On a concurrent matter, the federal law prevails to the extent of the inconsistency.
steps.result: The federal minimum standard prevails.

steps.reason: Federal supremacy is not unlimited: it applies only where the two laws are inconsistent.
steps.result: The state may add stricter rules that do not contradict the federal standard.

content.question: Why is Nigeria often described as a federation with strong centralising tendencies? Give two reasons and one consequence.
hints: Military rule concentrated power and governed by decree.
Oil revenue and the Federation Account give the centre fiscal leverage over states.
A consequence is weaker state autonomy or persistent tension over revenue and jurisdiction.
